claims.text: HEA multilayer protective coatings resist time-dependent plastic deformation.
Compositional complexity is a primary cause of resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in HEA multilayer coatings.
Nanoscale layer interfaces are a primary cause of resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in HEA multilayer coatings.
Nanoscale layer interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Nanoscale layer interfaces inhibit diffusion-mediated creep.
Multiple principal elements produce severe lattice distortion in the HEA layers.
Severe lattice distortion increases lattice friction.
The high-entropy effect reduces atomic mobility.
Lattice distortion and multilayer interfaces synergistically impede dislocation climb and glide.
Multilayer interfaces impede atomic diffusion across layers.
The proposed structural features suppress grain-boundary sliding.
Under identical elevated-temperature creep conditions, HEA multilayer coatings will have lower steady-state creep rates than conventional monolayer coatings.
The steady-state creep rate of HEA multilayer coatings will be at least one order of magnitude lower than that of conventional coatings under the same conditions.
HEA multilayer coatings will have longer times to failure than conventional coatings under identical creep conditions.
The hypothesis applies to HEA multilayer coatings having nanoscale layer thicknesses and high-entropy compositions.
The proposed resistance may not occur in coatings with thicker layers.
The proposed resistance may not occur in low-entropy alloys.
At temperatures approaching the melting point, diffusion becomes dominant and may eliminate the proposed resistance.
The magnitude of creep-rate reduction depends on the specific alloy system and layer thickness.
